teaser: For a few minutes at dawn, Japan's sacred mountain turns the color of brick.

lesson.text: Red is not the color of Mount Fuji. Most of the year the mountain is gray-blue, or white with snow. But in late summer and early autumn, when the snow has almost gone and the sky is clear, the first sun can light the bare slopes for a few minutes. People in Japan have a name for that sight: Red Fuji.

The real title says nothing about red. It describes weather: a fine southern wind, a clear morning. Hokusai gives you three things only. A mountain, a sky, a forest. No people, no houses, no road. So how does so little hold your eye for so long?
The answer is in two slopes that do not match.

lines.label: The long climb
lines.text: The left slope starts at the edge of the paper and rises in one slow curve, getting steeper as it goes. Your eye travels it like a hiker, from the forest to the snow.

lines.label: The short drop
lines.text: The right slope is cut off by the border almost at once. The summit sits far to the right, not in the middle. That imbalance leaves the whole left half to the sky.

lesson.text: Hokusai pushes his subject to one side and gives the empty part as much weight as the full part. In Japanese design, the space left open is part of the picture.

This is not a painting. It is a woodblock print, made around 1831 by a team. Hokusai drew the design. A carver cut it into planks of cherry wood, one plank for each color. A printer brushed pigment on each plank and pressed sheets of paper on it by hand, rubbing the back. A publisher paid for everything and sold the result.
Prints like this one were cheap. In Edo, the city now called Tokyo, a sheet is often said to have cost about as much as a double helping of noodles. Thousands were pulled, until the wood wore down.

The deep blue of the sky was a novelty. It is Prussian blue, a chemical pigment invented in Europe, which had recently become affordable in Japan. It was stronger than the plant blues used before and did not fade as fast. Hokusai's publisher built a whole series around it: the Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, which this sheet belongs to.
With so few shapes, every decision of the carver and the printer shows. Nothing can hide in a crowd. Three places on the sheet tell you how it was made, and who made it.
A summit, a forest, a label.

spots.title: The last snow
spots.text: The white streaks running down from the top are not white ink. They are the paper itself, left bare. The carver cut around them, so the red block never touched these lines.

spots.title: A forest of dots
spots.text: Hundreds of tiny dark marks stand for trees. They are thick at the bottom and thin out as they climb, then stop. Without a single trunk drawn, you understand how high the mountain is.

spots.title: Title and signature
spots.text: The framed box gives the name of the series and of this view. The loose writing to its right is the signature. Around both, faint vertical streaks in the blue: the grain of the wooden block.

lesson.text: Hokusai was about seventy when he designed this series, and he changed his artist name more than thirty times in his life. The signature here says, roughly, “Hokusai, now calling himself Iitsu.” He claimed that nothing he had drawn before seventy was worth much.

Because each sheet was inked by hand, no two are identical. Some early ones are pale, with a soft pink mountain and less blue. Later printings, like this one, pushed the red and the blue much harder, and that stronger version became the famous one. Collectors still argue about which is closer to what Hokusai wanted.

The series was so popular that the publisher added ten more views, making forty-six. Most of them show travelers, fishermen or carpenters with Fuji small in the distance. Here the people are gone and the mountain is alone with the weather. Go back to the red now. Is it a color, or a time of day?

quiz.question: When can the real Mount Fuji look red?
options: At sunrise in late summer or early autumn
quiz.explanation: With little snow and a clear sky, the first sun lights the bare slopes.

quiz.question: What are the white streaks of snow made of?
quiz.explanation: The carver cut around them so no color touched the paper there.

quiz.question: What was new about the blue in this print?
options: It was painted on by Hokusai himself
It was Prussian blue, a chemical pigment from Europe
quiz.explanation: It was stronger and more lasting than older plant blues.

quiz.question: Who cut the design into the wooden blocks?
quiz.explanation: A print was teamwork: designer, carver, printer and publisher.

quiz.question: Where does Hokusai place the summit?
quiz.explanation: The off-center peak leaves the left half to the sky.

facts.text: The Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji ended up containing forty-six prints.
facts.explanation: Ten views were added because the series sold so well.

facts.text: Every impression of this print looks exactly the same.
facts.explanation: Each sheet was inked by hand; early ones are paler, with a pink mountain.

facts.text: Hokusai designed this print as a young man in his twenties.
